newsitem.title: UK: UK's Brown to raise taxes, but by how much?.
newsitem.headline: UK's Brown to raise taxes, but by how much?.

text.p: As Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown prepares Britain's first budget from a Labour government in 19 years, the main question in most economists' minds is not whether he will tighten fiscal policy, but by how much.

Brown must perform a difficult balancing act, keeping Labour's election promise not to raise the overall tax burden on ordinary people and demonstrating that the party can make a difference to unemployment and the quality of key public services -- all while keeping financial markets happy.
If he can also persuade the Bank of England that he is doing something to dampen consumer demand, this could reduce the extent of the monetary tightening which also appears inevitable.

The new Chancellor's reforms at the Bank of England made it clear that he is not afraid of radical moves and raise the possibility that the first full Labour budget since April 1978 may be more far-reaching than financial markets expect.
However, the fact that Brown will have had little time to prepare for his first big moment at the despatch box could suggest a more modest package is likely.

Brown limited his room for manoeuvre before the May 1 election by promising not to increase the standard or top rates of income tax and to live within tight spending limits set by his Conservative predecessor Kenneth Clarke.
Nevertheless, Roger Bootle and Jonathan Loynes of HSBC Markets say there is little the Chancellor cannot do and there are hundreds of tax reliefs and allowances he could target.

"The pre-election promises not to raise the basic and higher rates of income tax do not bind Mr Brown's hands to any significant extent -- after all the last government enacted a huge fiscal tightening in the two 1993 budgets without touching either of those rates," they wrote in their budget study.
Brown's only other firm promise was not to extend value-added tax to food, children's clothes, books or public transport.
"From a macro-economic point of view, it makes most sense to target the personal sector, since this is the side of the economy which needs cooling down," Bootle and Loynes wrote.
"We continue to expect a fiscal tightening of four billion stg at the forthcoming budget, with a significant proportion aimed at the personal sector."

The main arguments in favour of a fiscal tightening are that the public sector borrowing requirement (budget deficit) is too high for this stage of the economic cycle and that higher taxes would reduce the need for tighter monetary policy that could put more damaging upward pressure on the pound.
Michael Saunders of Salomon Brothers expects modest extra restraint this year and a four billion stg tightening for 1998/99, one to two billion of which would hit consumers.
"Such a package would not hit the economy sharply and hence base rates will probably rise to about 6.75 percent in coming months to cut overheating risks," he said. Base rates are now 6.25 percent.
During the election campaign, Labour said its first budget would be a "welfare-to-work" budget.

The centrepiece will be a one-off "windfall tax" on the profits of privatised utility companies, expected to raise three to five billion stg which will be used to take 250,000 people off the unemployment register.
Many analysts expect a cut in advance corporation tax (ACT), which, perversely, raises revenue by reducing the tax credits companies receive on dividend payments.

If he wants to maintain his reputation for radicalism, Brown may make some move towards introducing a 10 percent starting rate of income tax, although this would have to be offset by extra revenue from elsewhere.
"In such a scenario, the most likely source of revenue would be to limit tax relief on allowances to the basic rate, raising some two billion stg," said James Barty of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Tax relief on mortgage interest payments is expected to be reduced or abolished outright.
"The phasing out of mortgage interest relief can be portrayed as an alternative to higher interest rates and as a method of preventing the housing market from getting out of control," Barty said.

A notable dissenting voice in the run-up to the budget came from the Institute for Fiscal Studies and Goldman Sachs, who argued that the public finances are in fairly healthy shape and there is no pressing need to raise taxes.
Tax revenue is already set to rise as a result of economic growth while public spending plans inherited from the Conservatives contain significant fiscal tightening, they said.

"We are tightening by about one percent of GDP per year," Goldman Sachs chief international economist Gavyn Davies said last week. "We do not actually think there is a major problem with the budget deficit at the moment."

On the other side of the fence, economists at HSBC James Capel say the fact that Labour has inherited a booming economy, with low inflation and sound public finances, provides a rare opportunity to present a radical reforming budget.
They urge radical reform of the structure of corporation tax to end what they see as a current bias against investment, together with a seven billion stg package of increased personal taxes.
"A radical, reforming but restrictive budget would also be taken very well by the markets, whose confidence Mr Brown needs to maintain if he is to lower the cost of capital," HSBC James Capel said.
